title: Ruth: From Loss to a New Beginning
lead: God can write a new chapter even when we have lost our home, our security and our future.
questions: Over whom do you speak pious wishes, when God is waiting for you to become the answer to them?
Do you let yourself and others speak to God bitterly and honestly, or do you insist on pious makeup?
Whose new chapter could you become the beginning of through a single decision: to go along, to let someone glean, to spread your cloak?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: The Book of Ruth records not a single miracle, and that is on purpose. The text describes nothing but human decisions, and God works from the inside, woven through them. The book opens with a sentence tinged with bitter irony: in Bethlehem, the “house of bread,” there was no bread. Elimelech took his family to Moab, and in time he died there, and so did his two sons. Ten years later Naomi was heading back to Bethlehem with no visible hope of a new beginning. The text doesn’t say what she expected. To the townspeople she said it straight out: “Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me. I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.” We need to underline something that is said far too rarely: Scripture never scolds her for that bitterness. In the Bible, lament is not a defect of faith, and God’s silence is not His absence.

One daughter-in-law, a Moabite, stayed with Naomi. Her vow is one of the most moving in Scripture: “wherever you go, I will go… your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.” She wasn’t choosing a husband. She chose Naomi’s God and walked off with nothing, toward poverty. So the two of them could survive, Ruth went to glean, and she “happened to come” to the field of Boaz, a relative of Elimelech. In this book, providence looks exactly like coincidence. Boaz did more for Ruth than the gleaning law for the poor required, and his first words to her were a blessing: “May the LORD repay your work… the God of Israel, under whose wings you have taken refuge.” On the threshing floor Ruth would answer him in his own language: “Spread the corner of your garment over me,” because in Hebrew “corner of a garment” and “wing” are the same word. God answers our prayers for people with our own hands.

At the city gate, the nearer relative counted the cost and declined to redeem; he stays nameless in this story. Boaz didn’t calculate: he took the field, the obligations and Ruth. The book that began with three graves ends with a child in Naomi’s lap and the words of the women of Bethlehem about a daughter-in-law “better to you than seven sons.” The little boy named Obed later became David’s grandfather. God built the royal line of the Messiah with the help of a Moabite widow who came from nowhere and had lost everything. A new chapter rarely begins with a miracle. It begins with someone’s decision.

Today we begin the section “There Is Hope When Life Falls Apart.” We step down from the stage of great events: after the battles of the judges we stay in the same era, but we walk into an ordinary home, a barley field, a town gate. The whole Book of Ruth records not a single miracle, and that is on purpose. No one sees a burning bush, no sea splits, no manna falls. The entire plot is made of human decisions: someone stays, someone goes back, someone lets a woman glean, someone goes to the gate. God works from the inside, woven through those decisions. This book was written for everyone whose life has fallen apart and who can’t see a miracle anywhere on the horizon.

sections.heading: The House of Bread Without Bread
paragraphs: The story opens with a sentence tinged with bitter irony: “there was a famine in the land. And a certain man from Bethlehem in Judah, with his wife and two sons, went to reside in the land of Moab.” Bethlehem means “house of bread.” The house of bread ran out of bread, so Elimelech, whose name means “my God is king,” takes his family to pagan Moab. The stay was supposed to be temporary, but it stretched to ten years. In that time Naomi buried her husband and both her sons and was left, as the text says, “without her two sons and without her husband,” in a country that was never meant to be home. Three graves in a foreign land, two widowed Moabite daughters-in-law, and no future. When word reached her that there was bread in Bethlehem again, she set out for home. The text doesn’t say what hope she carried with her. She herself will say only that she went away full and came back empty.

sections.heading: Call Me Mara
paragraphs: At the gate of Bethlehem the whole town is stirred to greet her, and she answers with a sentence that makes this book painfully true: “Do not call me Naomi… Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me. I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.” Naomi means “pleasant”; Mara means “bitter.” This woman doesn’t recite pious formulas about God’s will. She tells people to their faces that she is empty, and she aims her grief out loud at Heaven, in the language Job used to lament. We need to underline something that churches talk about far too rarely: Scripture never scolds her for it. In the Bible, lament is not a defect of faith. Naomi belongs, together with Job, the psalmists and Jeremiah, to those who were honest with the Lord in their suffering, and God accepted it. She may have experienced silence from Him, but the Creator’s silence is not His absence. The rest of this book proves it.

sections.heading: Your God Will Be My God
paragraphs: On the way, Naomi tries to send both daughters-in-law back to their mothers. Humanly speaking she is right: with her they have no chance at a good life. Orpah thinks it over and goes back, and it’s only fair to say the text doesn’t criticize her by a single word; she leaves with a blessing, as a good daughter-in-law. But Ruth stays, and she makes one of the most moving vows in all of Scripture: “wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God. Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried.” Look at what this young widow is doing. She gives up her home, her nation, the religion of her ancestors, even a grave in her homeland, and binds herself for life and death to an old, embittered woman with no prospects at all. Abraham once took a similar step, but he left with wealth and promises; Ruth leaves with nothing, heading toward poverty. And one more thing: she isn’t choosing a husband, because there is none on the horizon. She chooses Naomi’s God, whom she came to know in this family’s worst years. Someone in that house of mourning must have lived in such a way that a Moabite woman concluded: this God is real even when everything is falling apart.

sections.heading: She Happened to Come
paragraphs: Chapter two opens with a sentence that is the theology of this book in a nutshell. Ruth went out to glean, “and she happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelech.” She happened to come. The narrator deliberately uses a word that means chance, and lets us smile, because the narrator and the reader both know that nothing in this story happens by chance. In the Book of Ruth, providence looks exactly like coincidence, and from the outside you can’t tell the two apart. Gleaning behind the harvesters was the right of the poor, of widows and of foreigners, written into the Law of Moses. But for a young foreign woman with no protector it was also a risky business. The text notes no fewer than four times how Boaz looks out for her safety: he tells her to stay close to his young women and forbids the harvesters to touch or humiliate her. And then he does more than the Law requires: he lets her glean among the sheaves, drink from his workers’ jars and sit down to their meal. The Law sets the minimum of kindness. Boaz stretches it. In a book without miracles, this is what God’s care looks like: it has someone’s name, someone’s field and someone’s orders to the harvesters.

The text has a special word for this, one that ties the whole plot together: chesed, gracious, faithful kindness. Naomi had already used it on the road from Moab: “May the LORD show you loving devotion, as you have shown to your dead and to me.” In her mouth this isn’t theory: two pagan daughters-in-law had been showing her God’s kindness through all the years when she was sure the Creator had forgotten her. That is how chesed works in this story. God’s grace flows to a person through other people, including people from outside Israel, and it is this, not any miracle, that carries the plot from death to life.

sections.heading: Under His Wings
paragraphs: At their first meeting Boaz blesses Ruth with these words: “May the LORD repay your work, and may you receive a rich reward from the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have taken refuge.” A beautiful, pious wish. But at night on the threshing floor, when Naomi sends Ruth to ask for redemption, Ruth will say to Boaz: “Spread the corner of your garment over me, for you are a kinsman-redeemer.” In Hebrew one word means both “corner of a garment” and “wing.” So Ruth speaks to Boaz in his own words: you wished me refuge under God’s wings; be that wing. And this is one of the most important lessons of this book for every church: the Lord has a habit of answering our prayers for people with our own hands. Whoever wishes someone God’s protection shouldn’t be surprised to be asked to become it.

sections.heading: The Redeemer
paragraphs: The matter is settled at the city gate, before witnesses, because the gate was the court of that culture. Israel had the institution of the redeemer, the go’el: the nearest relative had the right to buy back family land. In this story a second matter had grown into the redemption: preserving the name of the dead. There was a relative closer than Boaz, and at first this relative gladly agrees to buy Naomi’s field. But when he hears that he will also be obligated to marry Ruth and raise up an heir for the dead man, he does some quick math: the Moabite woman’s son will inherit the land as the dead man’s descendant, and the costs will stay with him. So he gives up his right of redemption and takes off his sandal as a sign that he renounces it. For this the narrator hands out the quietest justice in the Bible: the man who wouldn’t preserve the dead man’s name remains nameless himself in this story. Redemption only pays off for someone who isn’t counting the money. Boaz didn’t care about material gain: he took the field, he took the obligations and he took Ruth, before witnesses, in broad daylight. In this scene Israel receives a deeply symbolic picture of the Kinsman who has the right to redeem and uses it out of love, paying a price He didn’t have to pay. When the New Testament calls Jesus the Redeemer, it will be speaking the language used at the gate of Bethlehem.

sections.heading: Better Than Seven Sons
paragraphs: The book that began with three graves ends with a child in Naomi’s lap. The women of Bethlehem, the same ones who heard “call me Mara,” now say: “Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a kinsman-redeemer… For your daughter-in-law, who loves you and is better to you than seven sons, has given him birth.” In a world where seven sons stood for the fullness of happiness, that is what they call a foreign woman who until recently had no children. The child is named Obed, and the genealogy adds one sentence that explains why the whole book was written: “He became the father of Jesse, the father of David.” The Moabite widow who came to Bethlehem empty-handed became the great-grandmother of Israel’s greatest king and, after Rahab, one more foreign woman in the genealogy of the Messiah. God built the royal line of His Son with the help of a woman who came from nowhere and had lost everything.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: If your life has fallen apart, this book tells you three things. First, you may speak the way Naomi did: bitterly and honestly, without pious makeup. God accepts lament, and He doesn’t show people the door when they say, “I am empty.” Second, a new chapter rarely begins with a miracle. It begins with someone’s decision: that someone will go with you, that someone will let you glean in their field, that someone will spread a cloak over you. That is why, in a church, each of us is a potential beginning of someone else’s new chapter. And third: between “I went away full” and a child in Naomi’s lap, nothing supernatural happened. There was only the faithfulness of two women, the generosity of one man, and God quietly weaving it all together. Up close, your story may look the same way: ordinary. Only from a distance can you see who was writing it.
